idiom_name: interface + default interface members / static abstract members (no instance state)
implementation_notes: The CLR will not give a value type zero size: the runtime pads an empty struct to one byte, and reference types always carry an object header, so a C++-style empty base cannot save storage here. Stateless behaviour is expressed with interfaces instead: interfaces cannot declare instance fields, so implementing one adds no per-instance storage (default interface members, C# 8, supply the bodies), and static abstract or static virtual interface members (C# 11) let a generic type parameter carry a stateless policy that is resolved at compile time with no instance at all. Use the interface form when instances must dispatch polymorphically; use the static-member generic form for pure compile-time policies such as operators, parsing or formatting.
pitfalls: An empty struct is not zero-sized in .NET (the runtime pads it to one byte) and it can add padding inside the enclosing struct, so 'empty marker' types are never free fields.

Static abstract interface members have no runtime dispatch: they are resolved through the type parameter at compile time, so they cannot be used as ordinary polymorphic instance members and require the generic-constraint form.
Calling interface members on a struct through the interface boxes it; keep stateless policies abstract or use the generic type parameter instead of interface-typed fields on hot value types.
